title: Image evidence: Fort Ancient (about 1000–1750 CE, northern and eastern Kentucky)
seoTitle: Fort Ancient image evidence: research notes
summary: Village farmers of the middle Ohio Valley who built circular plaza villages and low burial mounds, such as Cleek-McCabe and Petersburg in Boone County. Skeletal studies give actual heights and health data.
displayNote: This picture is an AI illustration reconstructed from the available archaeological evidence for the Fort Ancient period in Kentucky; details without direct evidence are informed guesses. AI illustration · Kentucky History Drive.

items.text: Petersburg study: men averaged about 5 ft 6–5 ft 7 in and women about 5 ft 3–5 ft 4 in; cradleboarding flattened the backs of heads.
Copper hair ornaments and rolled copper beads worn by a few people.
[Speculative] Tattoos, braided turkey feathers and stretched earlobes in the KAS portraits are borrowed from later historic accounts and are explicitly not known for Petersburg.

Hides and skins for clothing, footwear and bags; Indian hemp and native thistle fiber for cord, bags and clothing. Leather sewn with marginella beads in lines was preserved at a Jessamine County burial.
Disk shell-bead necklaces and bracelets, marginella beads, bird-wing-bone beads, pierced bear-canine pendants; after 1400, engraved rattlesnake and weeping-eye shell gorgets.
Bow and small triangular arrowheads; bone awls; mussel-shell hoes and scoops; ground sandstone discoidals; pipes.
Ohio River and Bluegrass valleys; circular village of bark-covered houses around a clean plaza with cemetery zone; corn, beans and squash; salt licks and cane.

No palisade or stockade is reported at Cleek-McCabe; the Kentucky Archaeological Survey describes a midden ring around a plaza, with low burial mounds on the east and west sides and the remains of one burned house.
In Kentucky, palisades encircled some but not all circular Fort Ancient villages; nearby Florence, of the same period, lacks one, while SunWatch near Dayton (about 1200) was palisaded.
Fort Ancient house walls were single-set hardwood posts (later sometimes set in wall trenches), mostly covered with bark, thatch or mats; wattle and daub is rare.

A woman about 5 ft 4 in at the edge of a circular Ohio Valley village of bark-covered houses around a plaza, in a fringed hide dress, with disk shell-bead necklaces and a copper hair ornament, grinding corn. Autumn hardwoods and river bottomland; no tattoos or headdress since those are undocumented here.
